contextTopics.label: Russlands Krieg gegen die Ukraine
background: Russland überfiel die Ukraine am 24. Februar 2022 in vollem Umfang. Vorausgegangen war die Annexion der Krim im März 2014 und der von Russland unterstützte bewaffnete Konflikt im Donbas ab April 2014.

Die UN-Generalversammlung verurteilte den Angriff am 2. März 2022 mit 141 zu 5 Stimmen und forderte den sofortigen Rückzug. Die EU, die USA und weitere Staaten verhängten seither mehrere Sanktionspakete.
Der Internationale Strafgerichtshof erließ im März 2023 einen Haftbefehl gegen Wladimir Putin wegen der Verschleppung ukrainischer Kinder.
Österreich ist militärisch neutral, beteiligt sich aber an den EU-Sanktionen und leistet humanitäre Hilfe. Waffenlieferungen erfolgen nicht.

contextTopics.label: Krieg in Gaza und im Nahen Osten
background: Die Hamas verübte am 7. Oktober 2023 einen Großangriff auf Israel mit rund 1.200 Toten und etwa 250 Verschleppten. Israel begann daraufhin eine großangelegte Militäroperation im Gazastreifen.
Der Konflikt reicht weit zurück: Israel wurde 1948 gegründet, es folgten mehrere Kriege mit arabischen Nachbarstaaten. Der Gazastreifen wird seit 2007 von der Hamas kontrolliert.
Der Internationale Gerichtshof befasst sich seit Dezember 2023 mit einer Klage Südafrikas wegen mutmaßlichen Völkermords; ein Urteil in der Hauptsache steht aus.

Zahlenangaben zu Opfern stammen je nach Meldung von unterschiedlichen Stellen — der von der Hamas geführten Gesundheitsbehörde, israelischen Angaben oder UN-Organisationen. Sie sind selten unabhängig überprüfbar.

contextTopics.label: Handelskonflikte und Zölle
background: Die USA erhoben ab 2018 unter Präsident Trump Zölle auf Stahl, Aluminium und zahlreiche chinesische Waren. China antwortete mit Gegenzöllen. Teile davon blieben auch unter der Nachfolgeregierung bestehen.
Die EU ist als Zollunion für die Handelspolitik ihrer Mitgliedsstaaten zuständig — Österreich verhandelt also nicht selbst, sondern die Europäische Kommission.
Zölle wirken auf zwei Wegen: Sie verteuern eingeführte Waren für Verbraucher im Einfuhrland und treffen Exporteure im Ausland. Wer die Kosten trägt, ist wirtschaftswissenschaftlich umstritten.

contextTopics.label: Inflation und Zinspolitik der EZB
background: Die Europäische Zentralbank hat als vorrangiges Ziel Preisstabilität, definiert als 2 Prozent Inflation mittelfristig. Sie steuert darüber den Leitzins für den gesamten Euroraum.
Nach Jahren mit Null- und Negativzinsen begann die EZB im Juli 2022 mit Zinserhöhungen, um die stark gestiegene Inflation zu dämpfen — ausgelöst unter anderem durch Energiepreise und Lieferengpässe.

Österreich lag bei der Inflationsrate über Jahre über dem Euroraum-Durchschnitt. Die Gründe dafür sind umstritten; genannt werden unter anderem Energiepreise, Mietanpassungen und der Gastronomiesektor.

contextTopics.label: Klimapolitik und Klimaziele
background: Im Pariser Abkommen von 2015 verpflichteten sich fast alle Staaten, die Erderwärmung deutlich unter 2 Grad gegenüber dem vorindustriellen Niveau zu halten und 1,5 Grad anzustreben.
Die EU hat sich auf Klimaneutralität bis 2050 festgelegt und Zwischenziele für 2030 beschlossen. Österreich strebt Klimaneutralität bis 2040 an — früher als die EU-Vorgabe.

Der Weltklimarat IPCC fasst regelmäßig den Forschungsstand zusammen. Dass die Erwärmung überwiegend menschengemacht ist, gilt dort als gesichert; umstritten sind Tempo, regionale Folgen und Gegenmaßnahmen.

contextTopics.label: Regulierung künstlicher Intelligenz
background: Die Europäische Kommission legte 2021 den Entwurf für den AI Act vor, die weltweit erste umfassende Regulierung künstlicher Intelligenz. Er stuft Anwendungen nach Risiko ein und verbietet einige ganz.
Das Gesetz gilt für Anbieter, die ihre Systeme im EU-Markt anbieten — unabhängig davon, wo sie sitzen. Die Pflichten greifen gestaffelt über mehrere Jahre.
Kritik kommt von zwei Seiten: Teilen der Industrie, die Wettbewerbsnachteile befürchten, und Bürgerrechtsorganisationen, denen die Ausnahmen für Sicherheitsbehörden zu weit gehen.

contextTopics.label: Österreichische Innenpolitik
background: Österreich ist eine parlamentarische Demokratie. Der Nationalrat mit 183 Abgeordneten wird alle fünf Jahre gewählt; die Regierung braucht dessen Vertrauen.
Der Bundespräsident wird direkt gewählt, ernennt die Regierung und kann sie entlassen — eine Befugnis, die historisch selten genutzt wurde.
Untersuchungsausschüsse sind ein Minderheitsrecht: Ein Viertel der Abgeordneten kann einen einsetzen, ohne Zustimmung der Mehrheit.

contextTopics.label: Raiffeisen Bank International
background: Die Raiffeisen Bank International (RBI) ist eine der größten Banken Österreichs mit Schwerpunkt in Zentral- und Osteuropa. Sie ging 2010 aus der Fusion von RZB-Teilen und Raiffeisen International hervor.
Der Raiffeisen-Sektor ist genossenschaftlich aufgebaut: lokale Raiffeisenbanken, darüber Landesbanken, darüber die RBI. Diese Struktur erklärt, warum Entscheidungen oft mehrere Ebenen betreffen.
Das Russland-Geschäft der RBI steht seit dem Angriff auf die Ukraine unter besonderer Beobachtung von EZB und US-Behörden. Ein Rückzug wurde mehrfach angekündigt und verzögerte sich.

items.title: The Organisation Owns the Minimum Definition of Done
items.summary: Originally published at Engineering Leadership on 21 October 2026 as The Organisation Owns the Minimum Definition of Done . The minimum Definition of Done exists to protect the business and its customers, so it belongs to the people accountable for them. Engineering informs it, and engineering should not have to set it: when it does, the business has given up a decision that is its own. Name the person who would answer to the board or the regulator if work shipped below it harmed a customer. If you cannot, nobody owns it yet. In the organisations I work with, the Definition of Done is usually left to engineering. It ends up describing what engineering can control (tests written, code reviewed, a pipeline passed) rather than what the business is exposed to. A leader reading it cannot tell whether the work protects customer data, meets accessibility duties, or keeps the company on the right side of its regulators. I have argued before that the Definition of Done should come from the business and be objective . Whoever owns the Definition of Done decides what happens when a deadline arrives When engineering owns the Definition of Done, I see three faults again and again. Scope gets in, as “meets acceptance criteria”. Numbers stand in for quality, as “80% code coverage”. Handoffs replace states, as “code reviewed” and “QA signed off”. Each of these is something engineering can tick without anyone accountable for the business looking at it. The more serious fault is what happens under pressure. A deadline arrives, the work is not ready, and somebody has to decide whether to ship. If the bar belongs to engineering, the pressure flows to engineering, and engineering is rarely in a position to refuse the people who set its deadlines. In my experience, the bar gets waived quietly once, and after that waivers become routine. My view is that whoever owns the bar decides what happens when it gets in the way. When the people accountable for the business own it, lowering it means one of them putting a name to that decision. That moves the decision to the people who carry the consequence. Many readers will hold a different model: engineering and the business own it jointly, with business sign-off. I think shared ownership leaves the bar negotiable between two owners at exactly the moment of pressure, and each can assume the other is holding it. One accountable owner, with engineering advising, does not have that gap. Engineers know how to achieve quality and how to show it. Knowing how is not the same as being accountable for the exposure. Leaders set the minimum; engineering advises on it and meets it. The Definition of Done is the minimum that protects the business and its customers What does the Definition of Done protect? In the organisations I work with, the answer usually includes security, privacy, accessibility, and legal and regulatory duties. The list is not complete. Each item is something the business answers for when it goes wrong, and each one is a duty to customers as much as to the company. It is a minimum, not a maximum. Products and teams go above it all the time, and they should. It is also never the whole of quality: a product can meet the Definition of Done and still be clumsy, slow, or unloved. For an organisation whose work is not yet live in production when it is called Done, I suggest something like this: Integrated into the main build, releasable, meeting our quality and security standards, and instrumented with telemetry that will support or weaken the hypothesis the work started from. Every phrase in that statement describes a condition of the work, with evidence attached to the work, that protects something the business cares about. None of it says how the team got there. Shipping work that is not Done harms the business and its customers Shipping work that has not reached the Definition of Done is a false value proposition: it looks like delivery, and I hold that it harms rather than helps. Low-quality work costs time, defects and money, and the studies below put figures on it. Tornhill and Borg found that low-quality code “contains 15 times more defects”, that issues took about 124% longer to resolve, and that maximum cycle times were about 9 times longer, though the authors work for CodeScene and used that vendor’s own measure of code quality [1]. Besker, Martini and Bosch reported that developers “waste, on average, 23% of their time due to TD” (technical debt), a figure the developers in the study reported themselves [2]. CISQ estimated the cost of poor software quality in the US at “at least $2.41 trillion”, with technical debt at about $1.52 trillion, a macro estimate that is not peer-reviewed [3]. DORA’s guidance states that “speed and stability are not tradeoffs”, which undercuts the idea that shipping below the minimum buys speed, though the finding comes from survey data and is correlational rather than causal [4]. items.title: Ethical Aspects of Using AI in Products and Organizations
items.summary: Image Artificial intelligence is increasingly helping us make decisions, analyze data, create content, design solutions, write code, and automate work. With the rapid development of generative AI, these capabilities are expanding at an impressive pace. In organizations, we therefore ask: What can we do with AI? How can we use it faster? Where can it bring the greatest efficiency gains? What value can it create for customers and for the business? What I observe, however, is that we ask less often: Should we do it? And this is where the conversation about ethics begins. My academic background also includes philosophy. I have spent most of my professional career in the world of technology, agility, and product management. Perhaps this is why ethics has never felt like an abstract branch of philosophy to me. I am primarily interested in it as a way of looking at decisions: what values lie behind them, who they affect, what consequences they may have, and whether we are prepared to take responsibility for those consequences. Together with Patricia Kong, I explored this topic in the whitepaper Ethics in Product Management [1], published by Scrum.org. Our starting point was a simple observation: ethics does not suddenly become relevant only when we build a product that uses artificial intelligence. Product decisions have always had an ethical dimension. Products influence people’s behavior, their choices, and their access to information or services. We decide what data we collect, what we optimize for, what behaviors we encourage, and who may benefit from or be harmed by the solutions we create. AI did not create the problem of ethics. What AI has changed is the speed and scale at which the consequences of our decisions can emerge. It also means that many of these questions remain just as important, if not more so. Ethics Does Not Start with AI When we start talking about the ethics of artificial intelligence, terms such as bias, fairness, explainability, privacy, accountability, or, more broadly, Responsible AI quickly come up. It is also worth asking a more fundamental question: what does ethics actually mean in the context of technology and products? In their day-to-day work, organizations look at decisions from several different perspectives. One of them is technological feasibility: can we build it? Another is whether we are solving a real problem and creating value for customers. Will customers want to use it? Does the investment make sense for the organization? Another perspective involves law, regulation, security, data protection, and compliance. In other words: are we allowed to do it? In my view, we also need the question raised earlier: should we do it? Organizations do not always ask this question and this is where we enter the field of ethics. Let us look at it from another angle. Not every feature we are capable of building should be built. Not everything that can generate profit should necessarily be implemented. And even compliance with the law does not automatically tell us whether a particular decision is ethically sound. The law sets boundaries. Ethics, however, helps us make decisions in the vast space that exists within and beyond those boundaries. There are different ethical theories and frameworks, which means that the same decision can look very different depending on the perspective we adopt. We discuss these approaches in more detail, with examples, in Ethics in Product Management . Personalization or Manipulation? Imagine a product that, with the help of AI, can predict with a high degree of accuracy which message is most likely to persuade a particular user to make a purchase. From a technological perspective, this may be entirely feasible. From a business perspective, it may look like a success. Let us assume that conversion increases and revenue grows with it. The way the system operates may also be fully compliant with applicable regulations. And yet one question remains: at what point does personalization become manipulation? If we know that a user is in a particular emotional state, should we use that knowledge to make a sale more likely? If an algorithm discovers that creating anxiety increases engagement, should we optimize the product in that direction? And if a recommendation system can keep a user in an app 20% longer, is that necessarily a good outcome? Who Are We Creating Value For? This leads to one more question I would add to the earlier ones: For whom? A product may create value for the company while reducing value for the user. A solution may be valuable for some customers while excluding a particular group. An AI-based recruitment system may reduce the time needed to review hundreds of applications from several days to just a few minutes. But do we know on what basis it rejects candidates? items.title: Customer Representative: The difference between a hobby product and something others might use?
items.summary: Image One of the things I’m trying to do as I develop Paper Drum is put into practice all the stuff that I’ve been doing over the last couple of decades in enterprise product delivery. Probably the thing that brings it all together in my mind is a training course that I’ve been delivering for some time called the Advanced Professional Scrum Product Owner class. This class doesn’t talk about theory at all. It assumes you know all that. Instead, it delves into the six stances of effective product ownership. I was delivering this class over the last couple of days, and I realised that when it comes to the customer representative and understanding customers, I’ve been breaking several of my own rules. Now, I’ve been quite deliberately following the advice that I’ve been giving. One of the key bits of advice is that you’ve got to get out of your own head. You’ve got to talk to real users and understand customers. And so, at a very early stage in the development of Paper Drum, I scheduled half a dozen calls with people I know: people I’ve worked with in the past, even family. People who are supportive of me, and therefore I can take their praise with a pinch of salt and try to tease out criticism. You’ve got to get out of your own head. Now, some of these interviews did prompt some useful information. For example, one user opened the product up - in my head, this was something that you would open up, you would play around with, you would improvise some melodies or some music or some drum rhythms. You would explore, you would be curious. But for somebody that had never seen my product before, they saw a piano keyboard as the first screen. Instinctively, they tried to play a tune that they knew, a simple melody, and they couldn’t, because it wasn’t set up that way. That wasn’t a good experience, and then they didn’t really know what to do. So based on that, I understood that it would be better to have some sort of introductory learning segments: somebody teaching you a rhythm, and then easing you into making up your own things. Another useful thing that came out of these interviews was a question I’d scripted, which did work quite well: “would you be prepared to use this for a week and give me some feedback at the end?” And somebody said, “Well, actually, you know, I’m supportive of what you’re doing, but actually, no, I wouldn’t. And the reason is that as it is right now, I can’t really see the point of it. There’s nothing to say why it would be worth it, why I would come back time after time.” As it is right now, I can’t really see the point of it. So that gave me really useful insights into developing something that would answer that question. What would I do? Why would I come back to this? That prompted me to build a learning pathway that would lead into the ability to develop your own rhythms, and then potentially share them with others, and then come back to it. But as I was teaching the PSPO-A class just over the last couple of days, and reiterating the advice about how to talk to customers, how to talk to users, I realised I was doing several things that I was telling the class not to do. I realised I was doing several things that I was telling the class not to do. Firstly, I was solving problems there in the call. At one point in the discussion, somebody said that they couldn’t see what they were supposed to be doing. Rather than just note that and thank them for the feedback, I proceeded to talk them through it and demonstrate. Now, this is a good thing to do, and I think any product needs effective support. You need a way for people to figure out what to do. But the trouble is that if you do that in a conversation where you’re trying to learn about what’s working in the product and what’s not working, that information then doesn’t come through. The focus of the conversation is “let me show you this” or “let me explain that”. That doesn’t leave space for “here’s what I think, this is my experience”. And that’s the stuff that you want. That’s the stuff I was looking for. The other mistake I made is that I was essentially pitching the product. I was explaining my idea of how music in the past was participatory. People used to join in, whereas now it’s more productised. It’s something you buy, it’s something that you listen to. And I was describing all the different options that I thought this product might be useful for. I was saying, well, it could be used in office teams, in groups. It could be used in meetings as an icebreaker, with groups of people making music together. Or it could be used as an individual activity: you might sit down and get into the right frame of mind before doing some work. And that meant that I wasn’t getting the sort of raw, unvarnished response. I wasn’t hearing how people received the product as it was. I also totally abandoned my plan to observe. items.title: Making Product Decisions Before the Results Are In
items.summary: Some product outcomes take weeks to become visible, yet stakeholders may expect decisions much sooner. For a Product Owner, the challenge is understanding what the available evidence tells us and how to make decisions when the intended results are still uncertain. Image When the evidence is not yet available During my work on investment management software, I was involved with systems that helped financial institutions manage investments and maintain accurate records. One situation that illustrates this challenge concerned the monthly process of checking investment records against information received from banks. We were developing a feature designed to detect differences earlier, reducing the manual corrections employees needed to make during these checks. After releasing it to a limited group of users, a stakeholder asked at the following Sprint Review whether we were ready to make it available to more customers. The initial numbers looked promising. People were using the feature, and the dashboard showed fewer manual corrections. However, most customers had not yet completed their monthly checks, meaning that additional problems could still be discovered. We knew people were using the functionality, but we could not yet establish whether it was reducing the work we intended to address. Understand what the numbers actually show Our dashboard showed the percentage of investment portfolios requiring manual corrections. A portfolio is simply a collection of investments managed together. The problem was that our calculation included portfolios whose monthly checks were still in progress. Those awaiting final verification appeared to require no corrections, even though discrepancies might be discovered later. Consequently, the results could look better simply because much of the work remained unfinished. After discussing the process with operations, we agreed to evaluate only portfolios that had completed their monthly checks, comparing their results with previous periods using the same criteria. However, the Developers identified another issue: some corrections were performed outside the application and never appeared in the dashboard. Even after the monthly checks were complete, our numbers could still underestimate the actual manual work involved. We were facing two different problems. Some results needed more time to emerge, while others were missing from our records. Waiting would address the first issue, but the second required improving the information we collected. Until both were addressed, the apparent reduction in corrections was not sufficient evidence that the feature had achieved its intended outcome. Decide whether to expand the release The stakeholder still needed an answer, and delaying the release also had consequences. I proposed keeping the functionality limited to the existing group until the next monthly checks were completed and we had addressed the gaps in our data. Other customers would have to wait longer for a potentially useful improvement, but expanding immediately would mean accepting uncertainty about its impact. That did not mean waiting regardless of what happened. If we discovered that the feature was failing to detect important errors, we would need to respond immediately rather than wait for another monthly cycle. Together with stakeholders, we agreed on what to inspect at the next Sprint Review, including the number of completed checks and whether we could account for corrections performed outside the application. Once we had reliable results, we could compare the manual corrections required before and after introducing the feature. Even then, differences in portfolio complexity or changes in working procedures could influence the numbers, so an apparent improvement would not automatically mean the feature was responsible. By keeping the release limited, we avoided extending the feature based on results we could not yet trust. We also identified gaps in how manual corrections were recorded, which gave the Developers and operations something concrete to address. Stakeholders understood why we needed more evidence and what we would examine before reconsidering the release. Whether the feature actually reduced manual work was still an open question, but we now had a clearer way to evaluate it. Make uncertainty visible at the Sprint Review The Scrum Guide describes the Sprint Review as an opportunity for the Scrum Team and stakeholders to inspect the outcome of the Sprint and determine future adaptations. A usable Increment can also be delivered before the Sprint Review, since the event is not a release gate. In our situation, the Sprint Review allowed us to inspect the released Increment and discuss what we had learned, including the limitations of the available data. As Product Owner, I remained accountable for maximizing product value and effective Product Backlog management, while the discussion with stakeholders helped inform our next decisions. items.title: Scrum and AI - Outcomes and Boundaries
items.summary: Outcomes, Not Automation Boundaries Before Acceleration Reflections on Agile, Scrum and Human Accountability in the Age of AI Overview Artificial intelligence is transforming how organisations develop products, make decisions and deliver services. Tasks that previously required weeks may increasingly be completed in hours or minutes. Yet faster execution does not necessarily produce better business outcomes. As AI reduces the cost of producing solutions, the ability to identify valuable problems, test assumptions and respond to evidence becomes increasingly important. To achieve true competitive advantage from adopting AI, organisations will need to develop the capability of learning and adapting at speed. This will require clear accountability boundaries and constraints, as well as holding people accountable to honouring these constraints. 1. Faster Delivery Is Not Greater Value AI can help us deliver so much more quickly. It can speed up all aspects of product development; however, increased output doesn’t mean improved outcomes. The rapid delivery can also create more waste. Poor products, difficulties in maintenance, huge volumes of text to analyse, and hallucinations resulting in flawed assumptions. I have witnessed the scenario where people use AI to generate a long winded email, only to have the recipient use AI to summarise it! Organisations must distinguish between producing more (output focus) and achieving better outcomes. The risk of generating a lot of low-value output is real. Agile principles become increasingly relevant because they emphasise customer value, feedback, collaboration and adaptation. The fundamental question is not how quickly AI can deliver, but whether what it delivers creates measurable value. items.title: Retrospective Actions Die at the Team Boundary
items.summary: Image In the retrospectives I facilitate, the same three notes keep coming back. The team has too much work. The plan assumed everything would go right, so every Sprint starts maxed out and work rolls into the next one. The third note is about shadow work, the favours, urgent requests and quick fixes that arrive from outside the team and never show up on the board. The team can fix the first two itself by planning less. Shadow work comes from people in other departments. Over more than twenty years of these sessions I have found that this kind of note outlasts the others, mostly because nobody in the room can say yes or no to it. The Ceremony Works Easy Agile's State of Team Alignment 2026 [1] surveyed 419 engineers, product managers and project managers. Of their teams, 61 percent rate their retrospectives as effective at finding meaningful improvements. Yet 69 percent carry out less than 60 percent of their retro actions before the next retrospective comes around. When Easy Agile asked why actions stall, it found that in 28.9 percent of cases the action needed a change outside the team's control, and in 20.5 percent it never made it into Sprint Planning. The report comes from a vendor of planning tools and keeps its method behind a sign-up form, so I read the figures as rough. Even so, the split between those two reasons matches what I see in client teams. In my earlier piece on Kata, I argued that retrospectives lack a method for the adapt half of inspect and adapt. That argument was about actions a team owns, roughly the 20.5 percent. The 28.9 percent is a different problem, and a better method inside the team does little for it. When the Action Stays in the Room An action that never reaches Sprint Planning dies inside the team. The Scrum Guide [2] already says the most useful improvements should be addressed quickly and "may even be added to the Sprint Backlog for the next Sprint." The Scrum Guide Expansion Pack [3], which I co-wrote, is firmer and says a team should not just talk about improvement, because Scrum "depends on meaningful, continuous improvement follow-through." Putting one improvement into the Sprint Backlog, with hours reserved for it, closes most of this gap. Chronic optimism widens the gap, because a plan that already fills every hour leaves none for the improvement, and so the improvement is the first thing to slip. Feature work usually has a stakeholder asking about it, and nobody outside the team asks how the improvement is going. Where the Other Actions Go The 28.9 percent bothers me more. Take the shadow work from the opening, and say most of it comes from one department that sends requests straight to individual developers. The Scrum Master raises it with that department's manager, who agrees it should stop. From there the request joins everything else in that manager's queue, with no due date and nobody tracking how long it sits. Two Sprints later the requests are still coming and the same note is back up. Each time that happens, the team learns that raising a problem changes nothing outside the room. After a few rounds people stop writing those items down. The retrospective then holds only what the team can fix alone, and those items do get done, which would explain how a team can rate the meeting as effective while most of its actions go nowhere. Inside the team, an action waits at most until the next Sprint Planning, a few weeks away. Once it leaves the team, there is often no queue at all, just a manager's good intentions, and the team has no way to tell whether the item is waiting or has been dropped. The Scrum Guide gives the Scrum Master this job and lists "causing the removal of impediments to the Scrum Team's progress" among the services to the team. The Expansion Pack is more specific and accepts that "some improvement actions rely on the assistance of Supporters," people outside the Scrum Team, and says Supporters show leadership by "supporting short- and long-term impediment removal." It also warns that practitioners too often look only at the short-term kind. What no guide can settle for a given organization is who receives the item and by when. Someone on the other side has to accept it, own it and set a date, and in most organizations only a manager can make that call. W. Edwards Deming separated common cause variation, which is built into how a system is designed and managed and so shows up again and again, from special cause variation, the one-off event like a flat tyre. A note that returns every Sprint is common cause almost by definition. Writing a fresh action item for it each time treats it as a one-off, the first of the two mistakes Deming warned managers about. He estimated [5] that 94 percent of problems come from common causes and belong to management, since only management has the authority to change the system. Chronic optimism is common cause as well, though there the system influences, often indirectly, the team's own planning. The Same Complaint,…

items.title: So entscheiden Sie, ob eine Initiative im Zeitalter der KI fortgeführt werden soll
items.summary: AI can shorten the time it takes to turn a proposal into something we can test. Once an initiative is underway, how should a manager decide whether to keep going, change course, or stop? I look at two things: the goal we’re aiming for and the evidence we use as a compass. Are We Getting Closer, and Is the Goal Still Right? First, I look at whether the initiative is moving us toward the goal and whether the goal is still worth pursuing. The same change can mean different things depending on what we’re trying to achieve. Comparing what happened with what we planned says little about why the work is worth doing in the first place. Use Business Value as a Compass Next, I look at how business value is changing. Are we delivering more value in the market? Is our organization getting better at delivering and improving that value? Both questions tell us what evidence to look for. It’s hard to establish how much value an individual feature created or which outcome a particular activity contributed to. When a leading indicator moves, the link to a later change in a lagging indicator is still a hypothesis. Comparing teams by productivity or by the value they generate, or checking whether work went according to plan, does little to answer whether an initiative should continue. This way of thinking comes from Evidence-Based Management (EBM). We set a direction, gather evidence through experiments, and use what we learn to revisit the goal or change our approach. EBM examines market value through Current Value (CV) and Unrealized Value (UV). It examines organizational capability through Ability to Innovate (A2I) and Time-to-Market (T2M). Read the EBM Guide Figure 1. The path to a goal can involve dead ends and backtracking. Evidence about market value and organizational capability helps us decide where to go next. Inspired by Figure 2 of the Evidence-Based Management Guide. Look at What Might Change and When The time it takes to see a response varies by initiative. Consider where a change might show up and when you might reasonably expect to see it. AI can speed up implementation. Customers and markets respond on their own timelines. At the outset, we may be unsure about both the goal and what to look for as a sign of value. Use the feedback you get to reconsider where you’re heading and what evidence you rely on to guide you. Set a Date to Review What You’ve Learned There’s a limit to how long we can wait for feedback. For each initiative, consider what might change and when you could reasonably observe it. Use that estimate to set a review date. This idea draws on the Agile Kata practice of setting an achieve-by date for the next target condition. Scrum uses recurring Sprints of a fixed length. Here, the review date is an opportunity to look at what has happened so far and decide what to do next. Set it for the initiative at hand and move it if the feedback and evidence you have gathered warrant more time. Explore Agile Kata Read the Scrum Guide Make the Decision When the Goal and Evidence Support It Deciding whether to continue, change course, or stop requires a goal that still makes sense and evidence that helps us judge progress toward it. Looking again at the goal helps us interpret the changes we’ve observed. Those changes can also prompt us to reconsider why we’re pursuing the goal. We need both to make a sound decision. On the review date, look at what you’ve learned so far. If you have enough evidence to decide, choose whether to continue, change course, or stop. If further observation would help, say what you want to find out and set the next review date. If you have to make a decision now, make clear which evidence you’re relying on. Figure 2. Bring feedback from experiments into the review. Inspired by the Experiment Loop in Figure 1 of the Evidence-Based Management Guide and the Agile Kata approach to setting dates.

items.title: Der Rahmen hält das Bild. Wie Sie es bemalen, bleibt Ihnen überlassen.
items.summary: Aus dem Scrum-Leitfaden: „Scrum ist ein leichtgewichtiges Framework, das Menschen, Teams und Organisationen dabei hilft, durch adaptive Lösungen für komplexe Probleme Mehrwert zu schaffen.“ Das Cambridge Dictionary definiert einen Rahmen als „ein System von Regeln, Ideen oder Überzeugungen, das verwendet wird, um etwas zu planen oder zu entscheiden.“ Schauen Sie sich an, was diese Definition auslässt. Es sind keine Anweisungen darin enthalten. Ein Regelwerk hilft Ihnen bei der Planung und Entscheidung; Es sagt Ihnen nicht, wie Sie den Plan ausführen sollen. Bei fast jedem Trainings- und Coaching-Einsatz werden mir die gleichen zwei Fragen gestellt. Wie sollten wir unser Product Backlog priorisieren? Wie sollen wir unsere User Stories schreiben? Der Scrum Guide beantwortet keines von beiden, und das ist Absicht. Im Unterricht habe ich das Wort in zwei Teile geteilt. Ein Rahmen ist in Cambridges Worten „ein Rahmen, der ein Bild, einen Spiegel usw. umschließt und trägt“. Es hält das Bild und unterstützt es. Es ist egal, was das Bild zeigt. Wofür ein Team Scrum einsetzt, ist ihm überlassen, ob es sich um Software oder eine Marketingkampagne handelt. Dann ist da noch die Arbeit. Sie können ein Bild in Öl, Aquarell, mit der Kamera oder mit einem Bleistift anfertigen. Der Rahmen wählt nicht für Sie. Was Sie machen möchten, bestimmt normalerweise, wie Sie es machen. Das Gleiche gilt für die Bestellung eines Product Backlogs oder die Beschreibung dessen, was das Team erstellen wird. Die Personen, die das Framework nutzen, entscheiden über das Wie, solange die Regeln, Ideen und Überzeugungen des Frameworks verwendet werden. Wenn der Leitfaden keine Antwort auf das Wie gibt, suchen Teams oft woanders nach. Sie leihen sich eine beliebte Technik aus und nennen sie Scrum. Story Points, User Stories, ein festes Retrospektivformat. Wenn die geliehene Technik nicht in ihr Bild passt, wird Scrum für eine Entscheidung verantwortlich gemacht, die es nie getroffen hat. Es zahlt sich aus, das Wie beim Team zu belassen. McKinsey hat herausgefunden, dass Organisationen, die ihre Mitarbeiter in die Lage versetzen, Entscheidungen zu treffen, mit einer etwa 3,9-mal höheren Wahrscheinlichkeit Top-Performer sind. Der Rahmen liefert dies nur, wenn das Team sein eigenes „Wie“ auswählt, nicht wenn ein Manager oder ein Tool es für es ausfüllt. Versuchen Sie Folgendes mit Ihrem Team: Listen Sie zwei oder drei Ihrer aktuellen Vorgehensweisen auf, z. B. wie Sie das Product Backlog bestellen, wie Sie Backlog-Elemente schreiben und wie Sie schätzen. Fragen Sie bei jedem einzelnen: Haben wir uns dafür entschieden, weil wir etwas herstellen, oder haben wir es von irgendwoher übernommen? Dann fragen Sie: Wenn wir von dem Produkt ausgehen würden, das wir herstellen möchten, würden wir dann den gleichen Weg wählen? Behalten Sie, was passiert, und wählen Sie eines aus, das Sie im nächsten Sprint versuchsweise ändern möchten. Ich hoffe, dass diese kurzen Artikel für Sie von Nutzen sind. Wenn Sie weitere Erläuterungen suchen, können Sie sich gerne an uns wenden. Sie möchten keinen dieser Blogbeiträge verpassen? Halten Sie wöchentlich die Serie „The Scrum Guide Explored“ in Ihrem Postfach bereit. Ich wünsche Ihnen eine inspirierende Lektüre und eine wundervolle Reise. Gedränge weiter! Bild
items.origTitle: The Frame Holds the Picture. How You Paint it is Up to You.
items.origSummary: From the Scrum Guide: "Scrum is a lightweight framework that helps people, teams and organizations generate value through adaptive solutions for complex problems." The Cambridge Dictionary defines a framework as "a system of rules, ideas, or beliefs that is used to plan or decide something." Look at what that definition leaves out. There are no instructions in it. A system of rules helps you plan and decide; it doesn't tell you how to carry out the plan. In almost every training and coaching assignment, I get the same two questions. How should we prioritize our Product Backlog? How should we write our user stories? The Scrum Guide answers neither, and that's deliberate. In class I split the word in two. A frame, in Cambridge's words, is "a border that encloses and supports a picture, mirror, etc." It holds the picture and supports it. It doesn't care what the picture shows. What a team uses Scrum for is the team's choice, whether that's software or a marketing campaign. Then there's the work. You can make a picture in oil, in watercolor, with a camera or with a pencil. The frame doesn't choose for you. What you want to make usually guides you in how you make it. The same goes for ordering a Product Backlog or describing what the team will build. The people using the framework decide the how, as long as the framework's rules, ideas and beliefs are used. When the Guide doesn't answer the how, teams often look elsewhere. They borrow a popular technique and start calling it Scrum. Story points, user stories, a fixed Retrospective format. When the borrowed technique doesn't fit their picture, Scrum gets the blame for a choice it never made. Leaving the how with the team pays off. McKinsey found that organizations that empower employees to make decisions are about 3.9 times more likely to be top performers. The frame only delivers that when the team picks its own how, not when a manager or a tool fills it in for them. Try this with your team: List two or three of your current how-to's, such as how you order the Product Backlog, how you write backlog items and how you estimate. For each one, ask: did we choose this because of what we're making, or did we take it over from somewhere? Then ask: if we started from the product we want to make, would we choose the same way? Keep what passes, and pick one to change as an experiment next Sprint. I hope you find value in these short articles and if you are looking for more clarifications, feel free to make contact. Don't want to miss any of these blog posts? Have the “The Scrum Guide Explored” series weekly in your mailbox . Wishing you an inspiring read and a wonderful journey. Scrum on! Image

items.title: Drei in USA Forschende ausgezeichnet
items.summary: Das in Nordamerika tätige Netzwerk ASciNA, das österreichische Forschende verbindet, zeichnet heuer drei Persönlichkeiten aus. Den mit 10.000 Euro dotierten „Junior Principal Investigator Award“ konnte heute Julia Brunner für eine Arbeit zum Zellstoffwechsel in Empfang nehmen. Die weiteren Preise (je 7.500 Euro) gingen an Lukas Altenburger und Matthäus Siebenhofer.

items.title: Fossil entpuppt sich als Urzeitreptilie
items.summary: Ein 156 Millionen Jahre altes Fossil aus den USA hat sich als unbekannte Reptilienart entpuppt. Sie erhielt den Namen Meilynodraco amonamarthi. Neutronenaufnahmen ergaben, dass der kleine „Drache“ nicht nur eine neue Art ist, sondern auch der bisher vollständigste frühe Vertreter der Choristoderen sowie ihr ältester Nachweis in Nordamerika.

items.title: Erdäpfel wachsen auch in Mondstaub
items.summary: Erstmals ist es einem US-amerikanischen Forschungsteam gelungen Erdäpfel in einer Mischung aus Mondstaub und Kompost zu kultivieren. Das nährt die Hoffnung, den Mond für die Landwirtschaft nutzbar zu machen. Für eine Besiedelung des Weltalls wäre das ein Durchbruch.

items.title: Wissenschaftler testeten 212 pflanzliche Lebensmittel. Jedes einzelne enthielt Pilzgifte
items.summary: Eine neue Studie hat ein überraschendes Problem aufgedeckt, das sich in beliebten pflanzlichen Lebensmitteln und Getränken verbirgt. Forscher testeten 212 in Großbritannien verkaufte vegane und vegetarische Produkte, darunter Fleischalternativen, Hafermilch, Mandelmilch und Sojamilch, und stellten fest, dass jedes einzelne mindestens ein potenziell schädliches Pilzgift enthielt. Diese als Mykotoxine bekannten natürlich vorkommenden Verbindungen können Getreide, Hülsenfrüchte und Samen während des Anbaus und der Lagerung kontaminieren.
items.origTitle: Scientists tested 212 plant-based foods. Every single one contained fungal toxins
items.origSummary: A new study has uncovered a surprising concern hiding in popular plant-based foods and drinks. Researchers tested 212 vegan and vegetarian products sold in the UK, including meat alternatives, oat milk, almond milk, and soy milk, and found that every single one contained at least one potentially harmful fungal toxin. Known as mycotoxins, these naturally occurring compounds can contaminate grains, legumes, and seeds during farming and storage.

items.title: Warum wirken Abnehmmedikamente wie Ozempic und Wegovy nicht bei jedem?
items.summary: Warum führen Ozempic und Wegovy bei manchen Menschen zu einem dramatischen Gewichtsverlust, bei anderen jedoch zu enttäuschenden Ergebnissen? Wissenschaftler untersuchen, ob die verborgene Energiesparreaktion des Körpers dazu beitragen könnte, den Unterschied zu erklären und wirksamere, personalisierte Behandlungen zur Gewichtsabnahme zu ermöglichen.
items.origTitle: Why don't weight-loss drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy work for everyone?
items.origSummary: Why do Ozempic and Wegovy produce dramatic weight loss for some people but disappointing results for others? Scientists are investigating whether the body's hidden energy-saving response could help explain the difference and unlock more effective, personalized weight-loss treatments.

items.title: Achtung, Hochwasser! "Keine Umwidmung möglich"
items.summary: Die neuesten Entwicklungen betreffend Rechenzentrum Stetten: Der ausgesuchte Standort Am Teiritz wird im jüngsten Gefahrenzonenplan als Gebiet für ein 30-jährliches Hochwasser ausgewiesen. STETTEN. Platsch! Da ist wohl einigen ein Stein vom Herzen gefallen. Durchschnaufen in Stetten. Aufatmen bei den rund 3.400 Bürgern, die auf einer Unterschriftenliste gegen das Rechenzentrum Stetten unterschrieben haben. "Laut Raumordnungsgesetz ist keine Umwidmung möglich", stellt Bürgermeister Thomas...

items.title: Warum riechen Fürze so unangenehm? Das Geheimnis braut sich in deinem Bauch zusammen
items.summary: Das Geheimnis hinter wirklich schrecklich riechenden Fürzen liegt in winzigen Mengen schwefelhaltiger Gase, die von Darmbakterien bei der Verdauung von Nahrungsmitteln produziert werden. Wissenschaftler enthüllen, warum manche Lebensmittel den Geruch von Fürzen verschlimmern, warum laute Fürze nicht immer am stinkendsten sind und wie sich unsere Nase entwickelt hat, um diese starken Gerüche wahrzunehmen.
items.origTitle: Why do farts smell so bad? The secret is brewing in your gut
items.origSummary: The secret behind truly terrible-smelling farts lies in tiny amounts of sulfur-containing gases produced by gut bacteria as they digest food. Scientists reveal why some foods make farts smell worse, why loud farts aren't always the stinkiest, and how our noses evolved to detect these powerful odors.

items.title: Die NASA beschleunigt Mars-Hubschrauberblätter auf Schallgeschwindigkeit
items.summary: Die NASA hat Rotorblätter von Mars-Hubschraubern erfolgreich mit Überschallgeschwindigkeit getestet, wodurch der potenzielle Auftrieb um 30 % gesteigert und ein großes Hindernis für leistungsstärkere Flugzeuge auf dem Roten Planeten überwunden wurde. Der Durchbruch könnte es Hubschraubern der nächsten Generation ermöglichen, schwerere wissenschaftliche Ausrüstung zu transportieren, weiter zu fliegen und Orte zu erkunden, die außerhalb der Reichweite herkömmlicher Rover liegen.
items.origTitle: NASA pushes Mars helicopter blades beyond the speed of sound
items.origSummary: NASA has successfully tested Mars helicopter rotor blades at supersonic speeds, boosting potential lift by 30% and overcoming a major obstacle to more powerful aircraft on the Red Planet. The breakthrough could enable next-generation helicopters to carry heavier scientific equipment, fly farther, and explore places beyond the reach of traditional rovers.

items.title: Warum Fettleibigkeit Männer und Frauen unterschiedlich betrifft, liegt möglicherweise in ihrem Fett verborgen
items.summary: Wissenschaftler der University of California in Riverside haben einen überraschenden Grund entdeckt, warum Männer und Frauen möglicherweise unterschiedlich auf Fettleibigkeit reagieren. In einer Studie mit Mäusen entdeckten Forscher, dass Immunzellen, die traditionell mit Allergien und Asthma in Verbindung gebracht werden, je nach Typ und biologischem Geschlecht entweder vor durch Fettleibigkeit bedingten Entzündungen schützen oder zu schädlichen Stoffwechselveränderungen beitragen können.
items.origTitle: Why obesity affects men and women differently may be hiding in their fat
items.origSummary: Scientists at the University of California, Riverside have uncovered a surprising reason why males and females may respond differently to obesity. In a study involving mice, researchers discovered that immune cells traditionally associated with allergies and asthma can either protect against obesity-related inflammation or contribute to harmful metabolic changes, depending on their type and biological sex.
